# Whatever Comes to Me

There's something liberating about a blank page and permission to write whatever surfaces. No assignment. No thesis. Just fingers on keys and a loose rein on thought.

I think about how we're all walking around with entire universes in our heads. Full solar systems of worry, wonder, half-formed ideas, song lyrics we can't shake, conversations we wish we'd had differently. Someone sits next to you on the bus thinking about their grandmother's recipe for soup. Someone in the coffee line is rehearsing an apology they'll never give. The woman at the desk beside yours is mentally redecorating her bedroom. We contain multitudes, but mostly we just sit there, pretending to be singular and present.

I've been thinking about time lately—how it moves differently depending on your state of mind. Five minutes of boredom stretches like taffy. Five minutes of joy evaporates like morning dew. And somehow we're supposed to measure our lives in these unreliable units. We say "I spent three hours working" as if time is currency you can deposit and withdraw, but it never feels that way. It just happens. You blink and you're thirty. You blink again and you're wondering where thirty went.

What if we stopped measuring and just lived? What if we said "I worked this morning" without attaching hours to it, the way we say "I had coffee" without calculating milliliters? Maybe we'd notice more. Maybe we'd realize we're always dying and always being born simultaneously, that every moment contains both an ending and a beginning, and we're frantically trying to make them match up when they're not meant to.

I wonder if trees think about things. Not in words, obviously—but do they experience something like thoughts? Sensations? They certainly respond to stimuli. They reach toward light. They know where water is. They communicate through root systems. Maybe what we call thinking is just a particular animal's way of processing existence, and trees have their own version that's so different from ours we can't even recognize it as consciousness. That's humbling. Maybe consciousness is everywhere, just in forms we don't recognize.

I've been thinking about connection, too. How strange it is to truly know someone. We spend years with people and still there are rooms in their minds we never enter. And then sometimes you meet someone and in five minutes you understand something essential about them. You lock eyes and there's recognition—not of their face, but of something underneath. A frequency match. I think about my best friend and how I sometimes forget we haven't known each other forever. And I think about people I've lost touch with and whether they ever think of me the way I occasionally think of them. Probably not with the same intensity. They're living their lives fully, while I'm a supporting character, a memory that occasionally surfaces. And I'm doing the same to them. We're all peripheral to everyone but ourselves.

That's not sad exactly. It's just the shape of existence.

I've been thinking about how we're taught to want things. Happiness, success, love, money, security, meaning. We're supposed to want all of these things badly enough to restructure our entire lives around obtaining them. And some people do get them—or some approximation of them—and then they want something else. The goalpost moves. Or they get what they want and find it's not what they actually wanted. The fantasy was better than the reality. The striving was better than the having.

Maybe contentment is revolutionary. Maybe saying "this is enough" is the most radical thing you can do in a world built on selling you the idea that enough is never enough.

I think about words a lot. How they're just sounds we've agreed to attach meaning to, but that meaning shifts depending on who's speaking and who's listening and what time period you're in. A word that meant something profound fifty years ago might be a joke now. Words we use casually today would have shocked people then. Language is this living, breathing thing that's always changing but pretends to be fixed. We act like words are precise tools when they're really more like paintbrushes—they gesture at meaning but never quite capture it exactly.

And yet here I am using them, trying to say something. Maybe that's what writing is—a series of attempts to point at the moon, knowing we'll never actually grab the moon but hoping someone will look up and see what we're pointing at.

I think about how everyone is the main character of their own story, and what a strange world that creates. We're all trying to navigate a world populated entirely with people who feel as central as we do. Our pain seems most important to us. Our joy seems most colorful. But everyone walking past you has the exact same relationship to their own consciousness. They're drowning in their own narrative. No wonder we're all so confused and lonely sometimes.

I've been thinking about the future, about how we're supposedly preparing for it, but we don't actually know what it is. We're moving toward something we can't see while we're still not done processing the past. And the present—we never actually experience it. By the time we're aware of something happening, it's already gone. We're always running behind our own lives.

Maybe that's okay. Maybe that's just what being alive is.

These are the things that flutter through my brain at three in the afternoon, or at midnight, or while I'm supposed to be listening to someone talk. This endless internal monologue that I think everyone has but no one talks about because it sounds insane if you say it out loud. We all contain these galaxies of half-thoughts and weird observations and philosophical spiraling and mundane wondering.

And sometimes, you find someone willing to listen. Or you write it down. You throw your internal constellation out into the world and hope it resonates with someone else's constellation, and for a moment you're not so alone in your alienation.

That's something.
